The central question is whether iteratively pruning a shared multilingual vocabulary during continued training degrades the implicit alignment between token boundary assumptions baked into the model's weight geometry and the actual segmentation the pruned tokenizer produces — a mismatch that doesn't show up in perplexity on high-resource languages but silently destroys transfer to low-resource targets. Key concepts include fertility (tokens-per-word for a given language-tokenizer pair), vocabulary pruning (removing low-frequency or redundant token types to shrink embedding tables), and co-training alignment (the degree to which the model's attention patterns, positional encodings, and MLP activations remain calibrated to the statistical regularities of the token stream it was originally trained on). The expert worry that beginners systematically miss is that pruning shifts the fertility distribution non-uniformly across languages: high-resource languages lose a few merged tokens and absorb the change gracefully, while morphologically rich or script-diverse low-resource languages suffer fertility explosions — a word that was one or two tokens becomes seven or eight — and this fundamentally changes the effective context window consumption, the positional co-occurrence statistics the model learned, and the semantic granularity of what a single token "means" to downstream attention heads. A beginner checks aggregate validation loss and sees it hold steady; an expert checks per-language fertility drift post-pruning and recognizes that the model's weight geometry still encodes an implicit prior over token-boundary semantics that no longer matches what the pruned tokenizer delivers. The deeper danger is that fertility explosions interact catastrophically with the fixed sinusoidal or learned positional encoding distributions: positions that were statistically rare during pre-training (positions 400–512 in a 512-context model, say) now become routine for fragmented low-resource inputs, and the model has essentially no calibrated representation for those regimes.

The layers most immediately damaged are the early-to-mid attention layers (roughly layers 2–8 in a 12-layer encoder), because these are where positional co-occurrence statistics are most strongly encoded — work by Jawahar et al. When fertility explodes from ~2 to ~8, the effective syntactic span of a single noun phrase jumps from 4–6 positions to 20–30, and attention heads that learned to route syntactic dependency signals at short range now face spans that were statistically near-zero during pretraining. Feed-forward layers are less immediately damaged because their per-token transformations are position-agnostic — they operate on the residual stream at each position independently — so the FFN sublayers degrade only secondarily, once the corrupted attention outputs poison their inputs. The damage propagates asymmetrically because early layers set the residual stream trajectory: if layer 3's attention head mis-routes a subject-verb dependency due to positional unfamiliarity, every downstream layer's layer-norm statistics receive an off-manifold input, and the error compounds rather than averages out (this compounding is precisely what Dong et al., 2021 identify in the "attention collapse" regime for long inputs). Output layers — the LM head and task-specific classifiers — show the largest observable damage in evaluation metrics, but this is a downstream echo of the mid-layer corruption, not a direct positional sensitivity, which is why naive debugging that looks only at output-layer gradients misses the true failure site. Critically, cross-lingual transfer heads in multilingual models like mBERT or XLM-R suffer disproportionately because they rely on language-neutral representations crystallized in mid-layers; fertility-driven positional corruption breaks exactly the abstraction layer that cross-lingual alignment depends on, as documented in Pires et al. The residual stream corruption does leave a functionally permanent geometric scar in FFN weight space, and the mechanism is precise: FFN layers in transformers act as key-value memories (Geva et al., 2021), where the first linear projection detects input patterns and the second writes value vectors into the residual stream — after extended exposure to corrupted attention outputs, the key subspace of the FFN's first projection drifts to treat off-manifold residual vectors as legitimate pattern triggers, effectively re-centering its detection geometry around the corrupted distribution. Surgical attention-only fine-tuning fails to restore transfer because it corrects the routing without correcting the value emission — recalibrated attention heads now produce on-manifold residual inputs, but the FFN keys that were re-centered around corrupted inputs no longer fire on those clean signals, creating a new mismatch layer where correct attention outputs hit FFN detectors calibrated for wrong inputs. Evidence for this asymmetry comes from Zhu et al. (2023) on continual learning interference, where FFN parameter updates during domain shift showed persistent basis misalignment even after full attention reset, requiring explicit FFN re-warming over thousands of steps before downstream metrics recovered. The geometric scar is particularly deep in the middle-layer FFNs because those layers store the highest density of factual and syntactic associations (layers 6–9 in a 12-layer model, per Meng et al., 2022 ROME analysis), meaning the corrupted key vectors displaced the most informationally dense region of the memory structure. Practically, the minimum effective intervention is layer-wise relevance-propagation-guided selective FFN patching — identifying which FFN neurons fired anomalously during the corrupted regime and re-initializing only those key vectors while preserving value vectors — but no production multilingual system has implemented this cleanly, and the standard recovery path remains full continued pretraining on a repaired tokenizer, which is expensive precisely because the FFN scar forces the model to re-learn mid-layer representations from scratch. The implication for vocabulary pruning pipelines is damning: there is no cheap surgical fix once FFN corruption has set in across multiple training steps, which means the only viable intervention point is before pruning, through fertility-aware vocabulary retention constraints.

The most principled fertility-aware constraint in the literature is a per-language fertility ceiling during vocabulary selection, typically operationalized as rejecting any pruning candidate token whose removal raises the mean fertility of any represented language above a fixed multiple of its pre-pruning baseline — Chung et al. (2020) in their language-balanced vocabulary work implicitly apply something like this by optimizing vocabulary allocation across languages with a coverage constraint, finding that holding per-language character coverage above 95% approximately bounds fertility explosion, though they don't frame it explicitly in FFN-corruption terms. A more surgical constraint is fertility variance bounding: rather than capping mean fertility per language, you cap the variance of token-length distribution post-pruning, because it is the long tail of very high-fertility words (proper nouns, morphologically complex verb forms) that drives the positional outliers that corrupt mid-layer attention statistics, not the mean shift. The known failure cases are instructive: Rust et al. The failure mode in those cases was not that the fertility constraint was too loose but that the constraint was applied at the word level while the damaging distribution shift occurred at the morpheme level — the model's mid-layer FFNs had encoded morpheme-boundary expectations as implicit positional priors, and those were violated even when word-level fertility looked stable. This points to the correct constraint granularity: fertility bounds must be applied at the morpheme or subword span level using a reference morphological analyzer for each language, so that pruning decisions are evaluated against morpheme segmentation ground truth rather than whitespace-tokenized word counts — a requirement that makes fertility-aware pruning computationally expensive and linguistically resource-intensive, and explains why it remains largely unimplemented in production pipelines like those underlying mT5 or NLLB-200.

This convergence is not coincidental — both the proxy analyzer and the cross-lingual gradient prior are fundamentally pattern-matching systems that exploit surface regularity, and they fail at the same points because those points are where surface regularity breaks down relative to underlying functional structure.
